description: Our goal is to develop AstroVital X, a system combining wearable health monitoring, NASA's Mars data, and intelligent mission planning to support astronauts during space exploration. We aim to turn creative ideas into real, working prototypes through teamwork and engineering.
summary:
AstroVital X is a wearable, locally connected mission-support prototype designed for astronauts operating on the surface of Mars.

Developed by Team MarsUp, it integrates real-time health monitoring, intelligent sensor reliability assessment, experimental navigation, and two-way voice communication into a single system.

An Arduino Nano ESP32 collects physiological, motion, and environmental measurements, while a Raspberry Pi processes telemetry and provides a mission-control dashboard. Our Sensor Confidence Engine evaluates measurement reliability, and HADSE provides explainable, rule-based decision support.

Through AstroHotspot, the Raspberry Pi creates an independent local wireless network, enabling live data transmission and functional two-way radio communication without internet access.

AstroNav provides directional guidance, alternative routes, and return-to-base navigation. Its current 10-meter target is designed specifically for live demonstrations, while future development aims to integrate actual Martian terrain data.

Inspired by NASA's Human Research Program, AstroVital X explores how astronauts can maintain situational awareness, communication, and operational independence during missions far from Earth.
details:
The Challenge

Human exploration of Mars presents major challenges in astronaut health monitoring, navigation, and communication.

Communication between Earth and Mars involves significant delays, making continuous dependence on Earth-based mission control impractical. Astronauts conducting extravehicular activities (EVAs) need access to reliable local information and communication systems.

AstroVital X was developed to explore how these essential capabilities could be combined into a single, locally operated mission-support platform.

Our Solution

AstroVital X consists of three integrated components: a wearable device, a Raspberry Pi-based local communication and processing system, and a mission-control dashboard.

1. Wearable Health and Environmental Monitoring

Our prototype uses an Arduino Nano ESP32 connected to multiple sensors:

  • MAX30102 for heart rate and estimated blood oxygen saturation.
  • MPU6050 for acceleration and motion measurements.
  • Magnetometer for directional information.
  • BMP180 for temperature and atmospheric pressure measurements.
  • SSD1306 OLED display for wearable information and navigation guidance.

Sensor readings are transmitted to the Raspberry Pi and displayed through the monitoring interface.

2. Sensor Confidence Engine and HADSE

Reliable measurements are essential when monitoring human health.

Our Sensor Confidence Engine assesses signal quality, data freshness, motion interference, and missing measurements.

HADSE uses these reliability assessments to provide explainable, rule-based decision support. It can identify measurements requiring additional review and avoid making recommendations when data quality is insufficient.

Personal calibration enables the system to compare new readings with an individual's measured baseline and flag repeated unusual deviations.

Mission Black Box records telemetry and mission-related events for subsequent review.

HADSE is a research prototype, not a clinically validated diagnostic device or a trained machine-learning model.

3. AstroHotspot: Independent Local Communication

One of AstroVital X's central innovations is its local communication architecture.

The Raspberry Pi operates as both a processing server and a Wi-Fi access point through a network called AstroHotspot.

Within the network's coverage area, the system supports real-time telemetry transmission and operational two-way voice communication between the wearable device and mission control.

This allows local communication to continue without an internet connection or immediate communication with Earth.

The current implementation has been developed and tested under terrestrial conditions. Its performance and reliability in an actual Martian environment have not been established.

4. AstroNav: Experimental Navigation

AstroNav provides directional assistance using compass and movement measurements.

The current prototype supports:

  • Heading-based destination guidance.
  • Approximate movement tracking.
  • Three alternative geometric routes.
  • Return-to-base navigation.
  • Directional guidance on both the dashboard and wearable OLED display.

A 10-meter destination is used specifically to demonstrate these capabilities in a controlled environment.

The long-term objective is to integrate real Martian terrain maps and elevation data to enable more advanced route planning.

The current version does not yet incorporate real Mars terrain datasets or provide validated absolute positioning.

Technologies Used

Hardware: Arduino Nano ESP32, Raspberry Pi, MAX30102, MPU6050, magnetometer, BMP180, and SSD1306 OLED.

Software: Python, FastAPI, React, TypeScript, JavaScript, SQLite, WebSocket, Arduino C/C++, and Vite.

Development Tools: Visual Studio Code, GitHub, Figma, and AI-assisted coding and debugging tools.

Scientific Foundation

Our project was informed by NASA's Human Research Program, particularly its research concerning the hazards and health risks of human spaceflight.

We focused on distance from Earth, astronaut health, and the importance of independent local operations.

NASA research publications were used to inform the project's problem definition and system requirements rather than as training data for an AI model.

Innovation and Intended Impact

AstroVital X combines several functions that would otherwise require separate systems:

  • Physiological and environmental monitoring.
  • Measurement reliability assessment.
  • Explainable health decision support.
  • Independent local voice and data communication.
  • Experimental navigation and return-to-base assistance.

Its local-first design reduces dependence on continuous external connectivity.

Although AstroVital X is not currently suitable for operational spaceflight, it provides an integrated research platform for exploring technologies that could support future planetary exploration.
